title: Three days in the river
hook: he walks into the river Bein to bathe and is not seen for three days

segments.voice: Yesterday: the modikhana, where the counting stopped at thirteen. Tera, tera, all yours. Today, the week's story turns.

Before dawn in Sultanpur. As he does every morning, the storekeeper walks down to the small river at the edge of town, the Bein, to bathe before the day begins. A servant waits on the bank with his clothes. Nanak steps into the water, goes under, and doesn't come up. The servant waits. Shouts. Runs for help. People come with ropes and nets; the governor himself, the story says, has the river searched. No body, no clothes, no trace. By evening the town has decided he's drowned. His sister grieves. A day passes. Then another.
screen: `BEFORE DAWN, THE RIVER BEIN.` → `HE GOES UNDER.` → `AND DOESN'T COME UP.`

segments.voice: First, plainly: nobody knows what happened in those three days. No hymn of Nanak's tells it. What there is comes from the janamsakhis, and Sikhs treasure it. They say he was taken into the presence of God and given a cup of amrit, the nectar of immortality, and he drank it. He was sent back with a charge: go into the world, remember the Name, and teach others to remember it. On the third morning he walked out of the river. Some tellings link this moment with the root verse from days ten and eleven; not every telling does. Sikh tradition remembers the river as the place Nanak's mission began. What it was like from the inside, the sources leave in the water. Look at the week that led here: a baby born in Talwandi, a sister who saw first, a boy asking what the letters meant, a cobra's shade, a true bargain, a storekeeper saying tera. All of it building, quietly, until one morning he walked into a river and came out someone the whole town would have to reckon with. A gurdwara called Ber Sahib stands on the riverbank today, and tradition says the jujube tree there, the ber, is the one Nanak sat under.
screen: `NOBODY KNOWS WHAT HAPPENED INSIDE.` · `A CUP OF AMRIT, AND A CHARGE.` · `WHERE THE MISSION BEGAN.` · `A WEEK THAT BUILT TO THIS.` · then, large: `SOME COME BACK CHANGED.`

segments.voice: Turn a tap to a thin, steady trickle, or sit by any running water, and listen. Bring to mind a time you went into something, a hard season, a loss, a long trip, and came out different. You don't have to understand it; just let the water run.
Bein. The river at Sultanpur where Nanak went under for three days and came out with a mission to teach the world to remember the Name.
Your line: some come back changed. Tomorrow, what he said when he came out. See you then.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember the Bein river as the place where Guru Nanak's mission began; pilgrims visit Gurdwara Ber Sahib in Sultanpur Lodhi and some bathe in the river.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: Vein, the river usually written Bein in English, at Sultanpur Lodhi.

what it means: three days in which, the stories say, he was taken into God's presence and sent back to teach the name.
what a scholar hears: the janamsakhis differ on the details; the Puratan tradition tells of the cup of amrit and the charge. Nanak's own hymns don't narrate the three days.
recall: the scripture honored as the living Guru

chat.says: What happened to Guru Nanak in the river? Did he almost drown?
options: He vanished for three days. The stories say he came back with a mission.
He nearly drowned, so he quit his job and never went near water again.
He wrote a hymn describing everything he saw during those three days.
chat.meaning: No one knows what happened inside. The janamsakhis say he was given amrit and sent back to teach others to remember the Name.

Bein.meaning: the small river at Sultanpur where Nanak vanished for three days

Sultanpur.meaning: the town where Nanak worked, and where his mission began

janamsakhis.meaning: the life-stories of Guru Nanak, told by early Sikhs
